nodes.label: Synchronous request/response (HTTP, gRPC)
nodes.rationale: Used when a human is waiting for a screen and an answer is needed now; cost is temporal coupling — both services must be up at the same instant.

nodes.label: Asynchronous messaging over a broker
nodes.rationale: Rule applied: queries go synchronously, state changes go asynchronously. Publishing RiskEscalated returns immediately so Risk is not as available as its least available dependency.

nodes.label: Command vs event distinction
nodes.rationale: An event is past tense, published, zero-or-many subscribers; a command is imperative, sent, exactly one handler. A 'command' with three handlers is an event with a misleading name and couples three services to a sender that thinks it talks to one.

nodes.label: Availability multiplies across sync hops
nodes.rationale: Five services at 99.9% called synchronously in a chain give ~99.5% — five times worse. Async makes a down consumer a waiting message rather than a failed request.

nodes.label: Temporal coupling
nodes.rationale: The real difference between sync and async is not speed but whether both services must be up at the same instant. Async moves the difficulty from availability to observability — a queue growing quietly at 3am is harder to notice than a 500.

nodes.label: Async is not fire-and-forget
nodes.rationale: At-least-once delivery with retries, a dead-letter queue and an outbox are required; 'async' without those is just losing data slowly.

nodes.label: 202 and honest intermediate state
nodes.rationale: Return 202 with the resource and let the user see the state change arrive; the mistake is pretending it was synchronous and returning a success that has not happened yet. The saga's POST returns Initiating rather than a fake completion.

nodes.label: Q5: REST API vs message queue / event bus
The five-minute downtime test
nodes.rationale: Ask: if the other service is down for five minutes, should this operation fail? Yes → call it. No → publish it.

nodes.label: How many services care, and will that change
nodes.rationale: With REST the producer would need N calls and know every consumer by name; with an event a fourth consumer is a new class in a different repository. The coupling difference is worth more than the availability difference.

nodes.label: Kafka vs RabbitMQ
nodes.rationale: Kafka is a distributed log with replay and offsets; RabbitMQ is a broker with routing, per-message acks and dead-lettering. This system needs routing and acks, so RabbitMQ.

nodes.label: Dead-letter queue and poison messages
nodes.rationale: Retry with backoff then dead-letter; never retry forever, because one poison message blocks everything behind it. The _error queue is the first place to look when a consumer 'isn't firing'.

nodes.label: Queue vs topic (point-to-point vs pub/sub)
nodes.rationale: Queue = one message one consumer, right for commands; topic/exchange = every subscriber gets a copy, right for events. MassTransit gives each consumer its own queue bound to the exchange, so both are available.

nodes.label: Q6: Advantages and challenges of microservices
Independence as the core advantage
nodes.rationale: Independent deploy, scale, fault isolation and team autonomy each have a precondition; a system where all services share a database has none of the advantages and all of the costs.

nodes.label: You replaced method calls with a network
nodes.rationale: Every challenge is a version of this one fact: the network fails, is slow and reorders, so you lose transactions and the stack trace and gain operational surface. Microservices trade development-time simplicity for deployment-time flexibility.

nodes.label: Distributed monolith
nodes.rationale: Distribution does not clean up a mess, it just distributes it. If the pain is 'the code is messy' rather than 'we cannot release without three teams agreeing', the trade is a bad one.

nodes.label: Concrete cost of this repo vs a monolith
nodes.rationale: 20 lines and one transaction become a saga plus 6 contracts plus 3 compensating consumers; one SQL query becomes a read model with 17 projections, an inbox and a rebuild endpoint.

nodes.label: Conway's law and rate/reason of change
nodes.rationale: Look for things that change for different reasons, at different rates, owned by different people — Conway's law and SRP pointing at the same place. Technical layers and one-service-per-table are the bad signals that produce distributed monoliths.

nodes.label: The redeploy test
nodes.rationale: Change this; what else must ship? If the answer is 'another service', the boundary is wrong. Companion tests: chattiness, transaction, vocabulary.

nodes.label: Risk vs Issues — similar tables, different contexts
nodes.rationale: They look identical but a risk register is reviewed monthly by a risk owner and an issue is chased daily against an SLA. The similarity of the tables is a trap.

nodes.label: Vertical slice as an extraction seam
nodes.rationale: A slice owns its whole path from HTTP to database, so 'which slices move?' has an answer. A layered codebase smears the use case across four projects and gives no seam.

nodes.label: Start coarse; merging beats splitting
nodes.rationale: Merging two services is much easier than splitting one, so start coarse and merge when two services are constantly chatty or always deploy together.

nodes.label: Ubiquitous language
nodes.rationale: Escalate, Materialised, Realise, Provision — the PMO's words in the code, not UpdateStatus and SetFlag.

nodes.label: Aggregate as a consistency boundary
nodes.rationale: One aggregate = one transaction. Things that must change atomically belong in the same aggregate and therefore the same service; aggregate boundaries are what cause (or avoid) distributed transactions.

nodes.label: No generic IRepository<T> over EF Core
nodes.rationale: DbContext is already a unit of work plus a repository; wrapping it adds a forwarding layer whose benefit is swapping persistence, which a service owning its own database rarely does. Being able to say why a pattern was skipped is worth more than applying it.

nodes.label: Anaemic domain model
nodes.rationale: A smell, not a sin. Risk.Escalate throwing once materialised is the single rule that stops a retried HTTP request starting the choreography chain twice.

nodes.label: Q9: Bounded context and service definition
Bounded context
nodes.rationale: A bounded context is the natural unit of a microservice: inside it the model is consistent and transactional, between contexts you translate and consistency is eventual. Never split a context across services; sometimes combine several into one service.

nodes.label: Why one canonical model fails
nodes.rationale: A shared Project class accumulates every field, forces lockstep upgrades (the monolith with extra steps), and is wrong everywhere — nullable fields mandatory in one context and meaningless in another.

nodes.label: Shared kernel (StrategyOps.Contracts)
nodes.rationale: Kept deliberately small — only the contracts — because every shared type is a coordination cost.

nodes.label: Anti-corruption layer
nodes.rationale: The rebuild endpoint's local Upstream* records deliberately avoid referencing other services' DTOs, because sharing DTOs between producer and consumer is how two services quietly become one deployable.

nodes.label: The linguistic test for a boundary
nodes.rationale: 'Project' means a stage machine with a sponsor and budget in Projects, and just an id and a code in Risk. Same word, two models; similar data is not a shared context.

nodes.label: Q10: What is an API gateway
API gateway (YARP)
nodes.rationale: Routes /api/*, validates JWTs at the edge, rate limits per user, and aggregates five services into one document in ~480ms so a mobile client does not make five round trips.

nodes.label: The gateway must stay thin
nodes.rationale: Business rules, data access and workflow orchestration do not belong in it: the moment business logic moves in, every team is blocked on one deployable and you have a distributed monolith with a fancy front door. The saga lives in the Projects service for exactly that reason.

nodes.label: Aggregation must degrade, not fail
nodes.rationale: Returning benefits.available = false beats a 500; an aggregation endpoint that fails on one unhealthy dependency out of four has multiplied the platform's failure rate by four.

nodes.label: The gateway is not a trust boundary
nodes.rationale: Anything on the network that can reach a service can call it directly, so every service re-validates the JWT. Trusting a header the gateway supposedly set is how one compromised pod becomes a compromised platform; the check costs microseconds.

nodes.label: Backend-for-frontend
nodes.rationale: One gateway per client type; a single gateway serving both ends up with query parameters that mean 'which client are you'.

nodes.label: Single point of entry vs single point of failure
nodes.rationale: A single point of entry is unavoidable; a single point of failure is a deployment choice — replicas: 2 behind a load balancer with a PodDisruptionBudget.

nodes.label: Q11: Service discovery and the service registry
Service registry
nodes.rationale: Services register on startup, heartbeat to keep a lease, and are evicted if they stop answering; addresses cannot live in config because instances change on every deploy, scale event and crash.

nodes.label: Client-side vs server-side discovery
nodes.rationale: Client-side: no extra hop, caller load-balances, every caller needs the registry client. Server-side: simpler callers, one more hop, and the balancer is another thing to run.

nodes.label: It is a lease, not a registration
nodes.rationale: A registry lists what has proved it is running in the last few seconds. Heartbeat at a third of the lease so two can be lost to a blip, and evict with a grace multiplier so a GC pause does not look like a death and make the registry flap. If a heartbeat 404s the service must re-register, not keep heartbeating into a registry that has never heard of it.

nodes.label: Ten-second lookup cache
nodes.rationale: Without a cache the registry sits on the critical path of every call and becomes the least reliable thing in the system. The cost is staleness, which the retry policy absorbs — the cache and the retry policy are designed together — and it makes a registry outage survivable.

nodes.label: Kubernetes makes the registry unnecessary
nodes.rationale: A Service gives a stable DNS name and load balances across pods, and readiness probes play the role of heartbeats — hence Discovery__Enabled: false in the k8s manifest. Building it once by hand is how you learn what the platform does for you.

nodes.label: Two-phase commit (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Holds locks across a network round trip so throughput collapses, the coordinator is a single point of failure that can leave participants blocked, every participant must support it (RabbitMQ and most cloud databases do not), and it couples everyone's availability.

nodes.label: Rollback becomes a business operation
nodes.rationale: There is no undo: the work genuinely happened and is genuinely being reversed, visibly. Irreversible steps go last, or use semantic compensation — not 'unsend the email' but 'send an apology'; the business decides what the compensation is.

nodes.label: Compensating action
nodes.rationale: Compensations should be simple and idempotent — delete a row and confirm — because a compensation that keeps failing is dead-lettered and needs a human on a genuinely inconsistent system.

nodes.label: The best saga is the one you do not need
nodes.rationale: Aggregate boundaries caused this distributed transaction; if two things must be atomic, put them in the same aggregate and the same service. A saga is the price of a boundary you decided is worth it, not a default pattern.

nodes.label: Saga pattern
nodes.rationale: A sequence of local transactions each with a compensating action; the answer to 'there is no distributed transaction'. Unlike a distributed transaction it is neither atomic nor isolated — each step commits and is visible immediately.

nodes.label: The three saga failure modes
nodes.rationale: A leg refuses; a leg never answers (a 30-second scheduled timeout compensates, otherwise instances stick forever); and a leg answers late, after compensation began — caught in the Compensating state and followed by a withdrawal, otherwise the scorecard survives attached to a project that never activated.

nodes.label: Every participant must always answer
nodes.rationale: WithdrawRiskRegisterConsumer confirms even when there was nothing to withdraw; answering only when there was work hangs the saga until its timeout. This was a real bug in the first version, caught by a test.

nodes.label: A business refusal is an event, not an exception
nodes.rationale: Thrown, it would be retried five times and dead-lettered while the saga waits for an answer that never comes, so the consumer catches the domain exception and publishes BenefitProfileRegistrationFailed.

nodes.label: Saga state must be persisted with optimistic concurrency
nodes.rationale: It must survive a restart — an orchestrator that forgets which legs succeeded cannot compensate — and three confirmations can land at the same instant, where without a concurrency token the last write silently discards the other two flags.

nodes.label: Semantic lock (the Initiating stage)
nodes.rationale: A saga has no isolation, so other services can observe half-finished state. Mitigations are semantic locks (the aggregate refuses most operations while Initiating), commutative updates, and designing so partial state is not harmful to observe.

nodes.label: Orchestration
nodes.rationale: One coordinator sends commands and waits for answers; the flow lives in one file and stuck instances are a table query. The cost is that the orchestrator knows every participant by name.

nodes.label: Choreography
nodes.rationale: Each service reacts to events and publishes its own; a fifth reaction needs no changes anywhere. The cost is that no file describes what happens, and debugging depends entirely on correlation ids.

nodes.label: Visibility versus coupling — the choosing rule
nodes.rationale: Orchestrate when the outcome must be all-or-nothing, choreograph when the reactions are independently valuable. A project with a register but no benefit profile is broken; a benefit flagged before the RAG moves is merely incomplete. Systems drift into choreography because publishing is the easy next step, which is the strongest argument for orchestrating business-critical outcomes.

nodes.label: The choreographed risk-escalation chain
nodes.rationale: RiskEscalated → Issues raises an issue → IssueRaised → Projects drops RAG to Red and Benefits flags the forecast; later IssueResolved closes the originating risk. Four services, no coordinator.

nodes.label: CQRS
nodes.rationale: Used here because the query spans four services and there is no join to write. Not worth it when read and write models are the same shape, which is most CRUD.

nodes.label: Read model (PortfolioScorecard)
nodes.rationale: Owns no truth — every column is a copy that can be deleted and rebuilt; written only by projections and read only by queries; eventually consistent, and the lag is shown deliberately. It keeps working when every other service is offline, which fan-out-per-request does not.

nodes.label: Carry resulting state, not just the delta
nodes.rationale: BenefitRealised carries RealisedToDate as well as ActualValue so the projection sets rather than adds; a redelivery with a fresh message id then cannot double-count. One contract decision removes a whole class of bug.

nodes.label: Derive counts, do not maintain them
nodes.rationale: Incrementing/decrementing RAG counters broke when a KPI recovered, because the projection could not tell a new reading from a moving one. Keeping a per-KPI status row and recomputing is self-healing; counters drift silently and forever.

nodes.label: Projections upsert, never insert
nodes.rationale: Events arrive out of order across five independent services — a KPI confirmation routinely lands before ProjectDraftCreated — so find-or-create makes ordering irrelevant except for fields that genuinely overwrite each other.

nodes.label: Rebuild the read model
nodes.rationale: A read model is a cache with a schema. Two honest rebuild routes: replay from an event store, or re-read current state from the owning services — this system does the latter because it has an outbox (a delivery mechanism whose rows are drained), not an event store.

nodes.label: Event sourcing (and why it is not CQRS)
nodes.rationale: CQRS separates read and write models; event sourcing stores state as a sequence of events. They pair well but each works without the other, and this system is CQRS without event sourcing.

nodes.label: Eventual consistency
nodes.rationale: Read-your-own-writes only holds by reading from the owning service, and monotonic reads need sticky routing or version checks. Being able to say what you cannot promise is worth more than claiming consistency is solved.

nodes.label: Transactional outbox
nodes.rationale: outbox_messages lives in the service's own database so the row and the message commit in one local transaction; a background publisher drains it. Order by an auto-assigned sequence not a timestamp; a failed publish stops the batch so a poison message cannot let later events overtake it; the message id is assigned once at enqueue time, which is what makes consumer-side deduplication possible.

nodes.label: The dual-write problem
nodes.rationale: Save-then-publish loses the event if the process dies in between; publish-then-save fires an event for a project that was never saved. There is no ordering of two independent writes that is safe.

nodes.label: Make the staleness window visible
nodes.rationale: A SignalR push and an 'updated Ns ago' column beat arguing: 'accurate as of two seconds ago' is a statement people accept, a silently wrong number is not. Design so the window is safe to observe — the project sits in an explicit Initiating stage rather than pretending to be Active.

nodes.label: Monitor queue depth, not just errors
nodes.rationale: A consumer down for hours is fine — messages queue and are processed on recovery — but a queue quietly growing at 3am is much harder to notice than a 500, and exceeding broker retention means lost messages, which is when the rebuild endpoint stops being a nicety.

nodes.label: The four resilience layers
nodes.rationale: Timeout, retry with backoff and jitter, circuit breaker, graceful degradation. The design question is not how to stop failures but what happens when this fails; underneath all four, asynchronous messaging is the structural answer, because you cannot make a synchronous call fault-tolerant, only make it fail better.

nodes.label: Bulkhead — one HTTP client per dependency
nodes.rationale: A shared breaker would let a sick KPI service trip the breaker for Risk too, turning partial degradation into total outage.

nodes.label: The thread-pool cascade
nodes.rationale: B slows down, A's threads block, A's thread pool exhausts, A stops answering anything including requests that never needed B. Timeouts and breakers exist specifically to stop this.

nodes.label: Degradation over failure
nodes.rationale: Returning four of five sections beats a 500; failing the whole aggregation on one unhealthy dependency multiplies the platform's failure rate by four rather than hiding it.

nodes.label: Chaos endpoints (/chaos/fail)
nodes.rationale: Resilience code is the least-tested code in most systems because its conditions are hard to reproduce, so triggering them was made a one-line curl. Measured: first call 1038ms, subsequent calls ~15ms with BrokenCircuitException, KPI unaffected throughout.

nodes.label: Q18: Retry and Circuit Breaker patterns
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
nodes.rationale: Handles transient faults — a dropped packet, a GC pause, a restarting pod. Jitter stops every caller retrying at the same instant. A retry is optimism.

nodes.label: Circuit breaker (closed / open / half-open)
nodes.rationale: Handles sustained faults by failing fast so the caller stays responsive and the dependency gets breathing room. A breaker is knowing when to stop being optimistic. Thresholds here: 50% failure ratio over 20 seconds with a minimum of 5 calls, breaking for 15 seconds — the minimum throughput stops one failure out of one call reading as 100%.

nodes.label: Resilience policy order
nodes.rationale: Total timeout → retry → circuit breaker → per-attempt timeout. The breaker must sit inside the retry so it sees every individual attempt; outside it would see one failure per operation and trip far too late. The per-attempt timeout innermost stops one hung request consuming the whole budget.

nodes.label: Retry 5xx only, and only what is safe to repeat
nodes.rationale: A 400 or 404 fails identically every time, so retrying wastes budget and multiplies load. Everything retried here is a GET; write paths go through the outbox and are made safe by the inbox instead.

nodes.label: Retry without a breaker makes things worse
nodes.rationale: A struggling service gets three times the traffic exactly when it can least afford it, and callers pile up until their thread pools are exhausted — the cascade by which one slow service takes down a platform.

nodes.label: At-least-once delivery
nodes.rationale: Exactly-once delivery does not exist across a network — it would need an atomic commit between broker and consumer database. Exactly-once processing does exist and is the consumer's job. Kafka's 'exactly-once semantics' is exactly-once processing within Kafka.

nodes.label: Inbox / idempotent consumer
nodes.rationale: The claim row and the business change must commit in ONE transaction; saving the claim separately opens a window where the service records 'handled' but crashes before doing the work, losing the message permanently. Keyed on (MessageId, Consumer) because one event often has several consumers in one service, and uniqueness is enforced by the database so two racing instances cannot both win. The table needs a retention job or it grows forever.

nodes.label: The message id is assigned once, at enqueue
nodes.rationale: Carried onto the wire deliberately, because MassTransit would otherwise mint a fresh id per publish attempt and a redelivery would look like a brand new message, defeating the whole mechanism.

nodes.label: Three layers of duplicate defence
nodes.rationale: The inbox catches the same message id again; a unique index catches two rows that must not both exist; a domain rule catches a business duplicate arriving with a fresh id. One layer is not enough because the inbox does nothing about a different message describing the same fact.

nodes.label: HTTP idempotency key
nodes.rationale: The client sends a unique header and the server replays the stored result for a repeat — what Stripe does for payments.

nodes.label: Q20: Securing microservices, JWT and OAuth
JWT
nodes.rationale: Signed, not encrypted — anyone holding it reads every claim, so it is not a place to cache a profile. Validation is a signature check against an in-memory key, which is what makes it scale and also what makes it impossible to revoke; hence 30-minute lifetimes paired with a revocable refresh token.

nodes.label: OAuth 2.0 vs OpenID Connect
nodes.rationale: OAuth answers 'may this application act on the user's behalf'; OIDC adds 'and here is who the user is' as an ID token. Authorization code + PKCE is the correct default; ROPC (used here for curl convenience) is discouraged in OAuth 2.1 because the app handles the real password, ruling out MFA, federation and consent.

nodes.label: Token relay between services
nodes.rationale: Forwarding the user's token means downstream services see the real caller and their real roles. Client credentials would be right for background work but wrong here — it gives every request the gateway's permissions and makes downstream logs say 'gateway did this'. The first version called four services anonymously and got four 401s.

nodes.label: Every service validates the JWT again
nodes.rationale: The gateway is not the only way in — another service, a debugging shell or an attacker past the edge can call directly. 'Inside the cluster' is not a trust boundary, and re-validation costs microseconds.

nodes.label: HS256 shared symmetric key — a known limitation
nodes.rationale: Every service needs the signing key just to validate, so any one of them could mint tokens for all the others, and rotating the key means redeploying everything. Production uses RS256/ES256 with a JWKS endpoint so rotation is a non-event.

nodes.label: Secure by default (fallback authorization policy)
nodes.rationale: A RequireAuthenticatedUser fallback closes any endpoint that forgets to declare a policy; forgetting [Authorize] is far more common than forgetting AllowAnonymous, and only one of those is a breach. Related: PBKDF2 with per-user salt and fixed-time comparison, refresh-token rotation as a theft signal, and roles as policies so adding a role changes one definition.

nodes.label: 401 vs 403
nodes.rationale: 401 means 'I do not know who you are'; 403 means 'I know and you may not'. Returning 401 for an authorisation failure tells an authenticated user to log in again, which in a browser is an infinite loop.

nodes.label: Independent deployment per service
nodes.rationale: One pipeline per service triggered by that service's path, so a change to Risk does not rebuild the other eight. If two services must ship together they are one service.

nodes.label: One image, all environments
nodes.rationale: Config from environment variables and secrets, never baked into the image; a separate image per environment means testing something you will not ship, and appsettings.Production.json in the image makes a config change need a rebuild.

nodes.label: Backwards compatibility for one release
nodes.rationale: Nine services cannot deploy atomically, so version N and N+1 run simultaneously: add a column before writing to it, add an event field before requiring it, never rename and replace in one release. Contract snapshot tests make that a conscious decision rather than an accident.

nodes.label: Expand/contract migrations
nodes.rationale: Three releases to rename a column, and that is the price of no downtime. It is also the real reason for the pattern: rolling back code does not roll back data, so each step must be independently reversible.

nodes.label: Rolling, blue/green and canary
nodes.rationale: Rolling is the Kubernetes default and what the manifests use, with maxUnavailable: 0 so new pods must become ready before old ones are removed.

nodes.label: Migrations on startup do not scale
nodes.rationale: Two replicas starting simultaneously both try to migrate and a failed migration crash-loops the pod; the fix is a Kubernetes Job or init container that runs migrations once before the deployment rolls.

nodes.label: Database per service
nodes.rationale: A shared server is a cost decision; a shared database is an architecture decision and a bad one. Compose runs one PostgreSQL server with seven separate databases.

nodes.label: Q22: How Docker and Kubernetes help
Docker (packaging)
nodes.rationale: Identical environments, per-service runtime isolation, second-level startup that makes autoscaling and rolling deploys practical, and immutable artifacts — the image that passed tests is the image that ships. Matters far more with nine services than with one.

nodes.label: Multi-stage build and cached restore layer
nodes.rationale: The SDK builds and the ASP.NET runtime image runs — about a fifth of the size and no compiler in production. Copying .csproj files and restoring before copying source is the single biggest win in .NET image build times. Non-root user turns a code-execution bug into a contained one for a one-line change.

nodes.label: Kubernetes (running services)
nodes.rationale: Takes over scheduling, restarts, load balancing, rollouts and stable DNS from the application. Not required for microservices — VMs with systemd, Azure Container Apps, ECS or Nomad all work — and adopting Kubernetes and microservices at once is two hard migrations simultaneously.

nodes.label: Liveness vs readiness probes
nodes.rationale: Liveness must not check dependencies: one database blip would restart every replica, turning brief degradation into an outage. So /health checks nothing and /health/ready carries the database check; a startup probe buys slow starters (EF migrations on boot) time without loosening liveness for the pod's life. maxUnavailable: 0 only makes rollouts invisible because readiness is honest.

nodes.label: Kubernetes Service and DNS-based discovery
nodes.rationale: A Service named projects-api is reachable at http://projects-api:8080 from any pod and kube-proxy load-balances across ready pods — which is why the hand-built registry is switched off there.

nodes.label: Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd)
nodes.rationale: Sidecars give mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and traces without application code, replacing the Polly policies and correlation plumbing. Worth it at large scale; a lot of moving parts before that.

nodes.label: Q23: Logging and monitoring in microservices
Logs, traces and metrics
nodes.rationale: Three tools answering three questions: what happened in this request, where the time went and which hop failed, and is this normal. You alert on metrics, because alerting on log lines drowns you. Debug order: metrics → traces → logs; going straight to logs is how you spend an hour reading the wrong service.

nodes.label: Correlation id propagation
nodes.rationale: Adopted not always generated, so a chain does not break at the gateway; pushed into Serilog's LogContext so every line carries it; returned on the response so a user can quote it; and written back onto the request headers so a reverse proxy forwards it — skipping that last step was a real bug. The broker hop is the one people forget, because a consumer runs on a thread with no HttpContext.

nodes.label: Structured logging
nodes.rationale: Message templates keep ProjectCode as a queryable field; string interpolation produces text you can only grep, and at nine services greppable text is not enough.

nodes.label: OpenTelemetry over a vendor SDK
nodes.rationale: Instrumentation should not change when the backend does — Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb or App Insights by changing an endpoint. MassTransit's activity source is included so a trace follows a request through the broker. Health probes are filtered out because they fire constantly and bury the requests that matter.

nodes.label: What to alert on
nodes.rationale: The four golden signals plus three microservices-specific ones people forget: queue depth and dead-letter count, outbox rows unprocessed and ageing (the earliest signal that publishing has stalled), and saga instances stuck in a non-terminal state. Alert on error rate, not an individual error.

nodes.label: Correlation id vs trace id
nodes.rationale: Both, and different: W3C traceparent serves tracing tools, while the correlation id is human-friendly, survives places trace context is not propagated, and can be read off a screen and quoted to support.

nodes.label: Q24: Migrating a monolith to microservices
Strangler fig pattern
nodes.rationale: A facade in front of the monolith lets one capability at a time be routed to a new service. Preferred over a big-bang rewrite, which means chasing a moving target with two systems to maintain. There is no prize for eliminating the monolith — stop when it stops paying.

nodes.label: Most of the work is untangling, not extraction
nodes.rationale: In the monolith, escalating a risk raises an issue, drops project health and flags the benefit — three services' worth of work in one method and one transaction. Someone has to find that method and every one like it and turn it into a message.

nodes.label: Split the data first, logically
nodes.rationale: The skipped step that stalls migrations: stop the rest of the monolith joining to a module's tables and force access through an interface. If you cannot do that inside one process you certainly cannot do it across a network.

nodes.label: Modular monolith as the honest halfway house
nodes.rationale: Sometimes the right place to stop. Stalling halfway is not automatically a failure — a monolith plus three well-chosen services is a fine architecture; the failure mode is stalling with a shared database, which is strictly worse than where you started.

nodes.label: Extraction order — Reporting first
nodes.rationale: Reporting is read-only with no writes to move and no consistency risk, so it proves the outbox, broker, pipeline and monitoring before anything that writes moves; then Benefits, KPI, the hard Risk/Issues pair, and Projects last because it is the hub. The goal of the first extraction is learning the mechanics, not delivering value.

nodes.label: What the migration adds that never existed
nodes.rationale: Outbox in every publisher, inbox in every consumer, compensation for every distributed operation, correlation ids and tracing, a read model plus rebuild, contract versioning, and per-service pipelines, dashboards and on-call. That list is the cost of the migration; anyone who cannot name it has not done one.

nodes.label: The bugs are in the seams
nodes.rationale: Almost none are caught by unit tests; every real problem came from running the system, not from a red test. Unit tests cover the least risky part, which is why the messaging tier is the second-largest test tier.

nodes.label: Bug: a silent saga participant hung the orchestrator
nodes.rationale: WithdrawRiskRegisterConsumer returned early when there was nothing to withdraw — which reads as sensible defensive programming and hangs the saga to its 30-second timeout. Lesson: in a saga, silence is a failure mode.

nodes.label: Bug: a projection that could not tell a recovery from a new reading
nodes.rationale: RAG buckets kept as increment/decrement counters broke when a KPI recovered, because the event carries the new status but not the old. Fixed by a per-KPI status row and recomputation.

nodes.label: Bug: a correlation id that vanished at the first hop
nodes.rationale: A reverse proxy forwards the incoming headers and nothing had written the generated id back onto the request. Lesson: a correlation id that is only logged locally is a request id; propagation has to be tested end to end.

nodes.label: Bug: provider behaviour invisible until it runs
nodes.rationale: SQLite cannot ORDER BY a DateTimeOffset, and only an INTEGER primary key autoincrements — which forced the outbox's ordering column to become its key. The fix belongs in shared infrastructure as a convention-applied value converter, not in each query.

nodes.label: Bug: shared code failing in one service and not its neighbour
nodes.rationale: An instance id truncated with [..48] throws if the string is shorter, and issues-api is two characters shorter than projects-api. That asymmetry is very hard to reason about from a stack trace.

nodes.label: Bug: the same identity bug twice, in two outbound clients
nodes.rationale: The gateway aggregation endpoint and, weeks later, the read-model rebuild endpoint both called downstream services anonymously. Lesson: when changing a cross-cutting concern, ask which other outbound clients exist — a grep for AddHttpClient would have found both in seconds.

nodes.label: The unplanned RabbitMQ outage that proved the outbox
nodes.rationale: The broker container restarted mid-verification; services stayed healthy, HTTP writes kept succeeding, two events sat unpublished, and the saga completed one second after the broker returned with nothing lost. Without the outbox those events would have been published into a dead connection and gone.

nodes.label: Build the platform before the second service
nodes.rationale: Outbox, inbox, correlation, health and resilience retrofitted across nine services is much worse than having them from the start, which is why they are the phase-1 commit. Also: start with a modular monolith, design events to be idempotent rather than only consumers, and write the failure test first — the saga tests written failure-first found nothing later because those bugs were never written.

nodes.label: The difficulty is operational, not architectural
nodes.rationale: The patterns are well documented and not hard to implement; knowing that a queue is quietly growing at 3am or that a saga has been stuck since Tuesday is the part that takes real work. Local development also gets heavier, mitigated by test tiers that need zero infrastructure and run in ~11 seconds.
